references.text: Background on the origin of the Samaritans: The Assyrian king settled foreign peoples in Samaria after the fall of the Northern Kingdom. They intermarried with the remaining Israelites and developed a mixed religion. This is the historical background for the hostility between Jews and Samaritans that the Samaritan woman refers to ([ref:2 Kings 17:24-41|2 Kings 17:24-41]).

When the Jews returned from exile and rebuilt the temple, they rejected the Samaritans' offer to help with the construction, which intensified the hostility between the two groups ([ref:Ezra 4:1-5|Ezra 4:1-5]).

Also during the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls, Sanballat from Samaria showed hostility toward the Jews, further highlighting the tension between Jews and Samaritans ([ref:Nehemiah 4:1-2|Nehemiah 4:1-2]).

The Samaritans refused to welcome Jesus because he was on his way to Jerusalem. This illustrates the mutual hostility between Jews and Samaritans that the Samaritan woman points out ([ref:Luke 9:52-53|Luke 9:52-53]).

In the parable of the Good Samaritan, Jesus deliberately uses a Samaritan as an example, which was shocking given the strained relationship between Jews and Samaritans ([ref:Luke 10:30-37|Luke 10:30-37]).

Of the ten lepers who were healed, only the Samaritan returned to thank Jesus. Jesus notes that it was only "this foreigner" who came back, highlighting the tension between Jews and Samaritans ([ref:Luke 17:16-18|Luke 17:16-18]).
The Jews used the word "Samaritan" as an insult against Jesus, showing the depth of contempt between the two groups ([ref:John 8:48|John 8:48]).
Jesus sends his disciples to witness in Samaria, breaking with the tense relationship between Jews and Samaritans that the woman at the well pointed out ([ref:Acts 1:8|Acts 1:8]).
Philip preached the gospel in Samaria, and many came to faith, fulfilling Jesus' will to cross the ethnic and religious boundary mentioned by the Samaritan woman ([ref:Acts 8:5-8|Acts 8:5-8]).
